messages.subject: cross-culturall validity lavaan
parts:
Hi,

I want to test a model with data that I have gathered in 5 countries. If I want to apply one model for this data I have to check measurment invariance for the contstructs that I have used. I checked measurement invariance for these four constructs but even no weak invariance can be assumed for all four!

My question is;
- Is measurement invariance necessary for applying one model in different countries (I think so)?
- Is there a possibility to correct for measurement invariance in lavaan and consequently use one model for the 5 countries. And if so where can I find more information/syntax?

Thank you in advance!
Kind regards,
Silke


This is my syntax for checking the measurement invariance of the four constructs, was this okay?
## Measurement invariance of the four construcst, group=country
# Model10: construct "Concern about marine environmental problems
myModel10 <- '
con=~q25_1+q25_2+q25_3+q25_4+q25_5+q25_6
'
# model 10a: configural invariance
fit10a <- cfa(myModel10, data=myData, se = "robust", test="Satorra-Bentler", group="Code_country")
summary(fit10a, fit.measures=TRUE, standardized=TRUE)
# model 10b: weak invariance
fit10b <- cfa(myModel10, data=myData, se = "robust", test="Satorra-Bentler", group="Code_country",
group.equal="loadings")
anova(fit10a,fit10b)
summary(fit10b, fit.measures=TRUE, standardized=TRUE)
# model 10c: strong invariance
fit10c <- cfa(myModel10, data=myData, se = "robust", test="Satorra-Bentler", group="Code_country",
group.equal=c("loadings", "intercepts"))
anova(fit10b,fit10c)
# Model11: construct "Industry=cause"
myModel11 <- '
caus_ind=~q22_1+q22_2+q22_3
'
# model 11a: configural invariance
fit11a <- cfa(myModel11, data=myData, se = "robust", test="Satorra-Bentler", group="Code_country")
summary(fit11a, fit.measures=TRUE, standardized=TRUE)
# model 11b: weak invariance
fit11b <- cfa(myModel11, data=myData, se = "robust", test="Satorra-Bentler", group="Code_country",
group.equal="loadings")
anova(fit11a,fit11b)
summary(fit11b, fit.measures=TRUE, standardized=TRUE)
# model 11c: strong invariance
fit11c <- cfa(myModel11, data=myData, se = "robust", test="Satorra-Bentler", group="Code_country",
group.equal=c("loadings", "intercepts"))
anova(fit11b,fit11c)
# Model12: construct "Human=cause"
myModel12 <- '
caus_hum=~q22_5+q22_8
'
# model 12a: configural invariance
fit12a <- cfa(myModel12, data=myData, se = "robust", test="Satorra-Bentler",group="Code_country")
summary(fit12a, fit.measures=TRUE, standardized=TRUE)
# model 12b: weak invariance
fit12b <- cfa(myModel12, data=myData, se = "robust", test="Satorra-Bentler", group="Code_country",
group.equal="loadings")
anova(fit12a,fit12b)
summary(fit12b, fit.measures=TRUE, standardized=TRUE)
# model 12c: strong invariance
fit12c <- cfa(myModel12, data=myData, se = "robust", test="Satorra-Bentler", group="Code_country",
group.equal=c("loadings", "intercepts"))
anova(fit12b,fit12c)
# Model13: construct "PCE"

PCE=~q24_3+q24_4

# model 13a: configural invariance

messages.author: 99a06696c483481a
messages.subject: Re: cross-culturall validity lavaan
parts:
Yes, invariance will be important if you want to compare the values of model coefficients across groups, but *partial* measurement invariance van be sufficient?  You need 2 indicators per factor (including the reference variable, with loading fixed to 1) to be invariant, not all of them.  If you can find 2 where invariance holds, then you have a basis for comparing model parameter estimates across groups.  Look for Steenkamp and Baumgartner's classic 1998 or 1999 Journal of Consumer Research paper.
--Ed Rigdon

parts:
Thank you for your help!

Just following question:
- Do you have to check (partial) measurement invariance for the whole model or do you have to check (partial) measurement invariance for your constructs seperately (as in my previous script)?
- I have no partial scalar invariance (but I do have metric invariance) and I cannot free any parameters anymore, I assume this is a problem for comparing means?

Thank you!

My script now (hence checking measurement invariance for the whole model):
#model
myModel2 <- 'con ~ caus_ind+caus_hum
PCE ~ con+caus_ind+caus_hum
PCE=~q24_3+q24_4
con=~q25_1+q25_2+q25_3+q25_4+q25_5+q25_6
caus_ind=~q22_1+q22_2+q22_3
caus_hum=~q22_5+q22_8'
# model 2a: configural invariance
fit2a <- cfa(myModel2, data=myData, se = "robust", test="Satorra-Bentler", group="Code_country")
summary(fit2a, fit.measures=TRUE, standardized=TRUE)
fitMeasures(fit2a, c("chisq", "df", "pvalue", "cfi", "rmsea", "srmr"))
resid(fit2a, "standardized")
subset(modindices(fit2a), mi>6)
#besluit uit covariances and modification indices: set free q25_1, q25_2, q25_5, q25_6! (evt q22_3, q22_5)
myModel2b <- 'con ~ caus_ind+caus_hum
PCE ~ con+caus_ind+caus_hum
PCE=~c*q24_3+c*q24_4
con=~q25_1+q25_2+a*q25_3+a*q25_4+q25_5+q25_6
caus_ind=~b*q22_1+b*q22_2+q22_3
caus_hum=~d*q22_5+d*q22_8'

# model 2b: weak invariance
fit2b <- cfa(myModel2b, data=myData, se = "robust", test="Satorra-Bentler", group="Code_country")
anova(fit2a,fit2b)
summary(fit2b, fit.measures=TRUE, standardized=TRUE)
#partial weak invariance! p>0.05
# model 2c: strong invariance: scalar invariance: only the incerpts of the invariant factor loadings were contrained to be equal across groups
myModel2c <- 'con ~ caus_ind+caus_hum
PCE ~ con+caus_ind+caus_hum
PCE=~c*q24_3+c*q24_4
con=~q25_1+q25_2+a*q25_3+a*q25_4+q25_5+q25_6
caus_ind=~b*q22_1+b*q22_2+q22_3
caus_hum=~d*q22_5+d*q22_8
q24_3 ~ 1
q24_4 ~ equal("q24_3 ~ 1")*1
q25_3 ~ 1
q25_4 ~ equal("q25_3 ~ 1")*1
q22_1 ~ 1
q22_2 ~ equal("q22_1 ~ 1")*1
q22_5 ~ 1
q22_8 ~ equal("q22_5 ~ 1")*1
'
fit2c <- cfa(myModel2c, data=myData, se = "robust", test="Satorra-Bentler", group="Code_country")
anova(fit2b,fit2c)
fitMeasures(fit2c, c("chisq", "df", "pvalue", "cfi", "rmsea", "srmr"))
resid(fit2c, "standardized")
subset(modindices(fit2c), mi>6)

messages.subject: Re: cross-culturall validity lavaan
parts:
If you don't check each factor, then there might be differences in parameter estimates because of differences in mean or scale for factors not checked.  I can imagine a large model where interest centers on just a few paths, and where some factors in another part of the model are not involved in those paths.  But I would want to be careful in reasoning through any such exclusions of factors, to be sure I had not missed something.
     Remember also that factor model results only apply within the context of a certain model.  If you evaluate each factor in a model by itself and get a certain result, there is no guarantee that you will get the same result once you bring the factors back together in a larger model.
